newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SBC Warburg appointed to value S.African Airways.
newsitem.headline: SBC Warburg appointed to value S.African Airways.

text.p: South African transport parastatal Transnet said on Wednesday it had appointed SBC Warburg to review and value South African Airways (SAA), earmarked by the government as a candidate for privatisation.
SBC Warburg will conduct the exercise in cooperation with two local accounting firms, Kessel Feinstein and N.N. Gobodo & Co. The process is expected to take approximately three months to complete.

"This valuation is regarded as an important exercise and the results obtained will serve as key inputs in determining the future strategic direction of the airline," SAA executive director Zukile Nomvete said in a statement.
The government has identified transport as the second sector for full or partial privatisation after telecommunications, where talks with potential privatisation partners are already well advanced.
Privatisation is viewed as a litmus test of the commitment of President Nelson Mandela's governemnt to economic reforms.

Hopes were raised this week that the process was firmly back on track following conciliatory remarks by union leader Sam Shilowa and news that a shortlist of potential partners for telecoms group Telkom could be announced as early as this week.

Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau said earlier on Wednesday that the endorsement of partial privatisation by Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) General Secretary Shilowa was to be welcomed.

Shilowa said on Saturday that Cosatu's national executive committee had accepted some state assets might require the involvement of private sector capital based on the need for new technology or the need for new capital.
"Where there is a compelling case for such an approach, the federation is willing to consider them. In such a situation, the state should remain the majority shareholder," he said.
Sectors which should stay in state hands, Shilowa said, included post and telecommunication, electricity, roads, public transport, health, water, municipal services and education.

Shilowa had made similar comments before, but the endorsement by the executive committee was seen as a further softening in union oppposition to privatisation, which Mandela declared in May to be government policy.
